header_text: Date: 2025-07-22 | Start: 16:00 PDT | Duration: 58m | Meeting: Lyra Bio POC - Quality Eval Playbook | Attendees: Redwood AE+SE + Lyra ML/Eng/Security
summary: POC scoping focused on defining quality evaluation plan: golden prompts, regression suite, hallucination/format checks, scoring metrics, workload sizing for smoke and pilot runs, and timeline for pilot kickoff. Discussed hosted vs dedicated, data residency, and security artifacts. Agreed action items and next steps.
topics: Workload sizing for smoke and full pilot
transcript:
[00:00] Priya Kapoor: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll cover the quality eval playbook and the POC sizing today, this is Priya from Redwood...
[00:18] Marta Villanueva: Great, thanks. We're mostly concerned with hallucination rates and format fidelity for our summary extraction models.
[00:28] Chris Lang: Cool, quick intro - I'm Chris, SE - I'll take point on the benchmark harness and the regression tests.
[00:36] Samir Patel: Hi, Samir here, engineering manager. Our target latency is sub-350 ms p50 for 512 tokens, and we need cost estimates.
[00:48] Priya Kapoor: Noted. For the POC we generally do a smoke run then a pilot - smoke is small but representative, pilot is 5k-20k prompts depending on throughput.
[01:05] Dr. Elise Cho: What does quality gating look like? We need concrete pass/fail so product can decide.
[01:12] Jordan Meyer: We recommend a hybrid gate — automated checks (format, exact-match fields, hallucination heuristics) plus human eval on a golden set. Example: < 2% hallucination on golden set and format error rate < 1% for acceptance.
[01:30] Marta Villanueva: < 2% feels tight but reasonable, can you explain hallucination heuristics?
[01:36] Chris Lang: Sure - two parts: 1) string-level verification against known-canonical answers for golden prompts, 2) embedding-similarity checks to identify off-topic completions. We also have simple named-entity checks for our domain terms. The heuristics flag suspect outputs for human review.
[01:56] Samir Patel: Will embedding similarity be false-positive heavy? Our corpora are noisy.
[02:02] Chris Lang: It can be; we tune thresholds per corpus. We combine it with rule-based checks — e.g., if entity present but numerical stats changed dramatically, flag.
[02:18] Elise Cho: So what's in a golden prompt set?
[02:23] Priya Kapoor: Golden prompts should represent critical user journeys: top-10 frequent prompts, edge cases, adversarial prompts, and format-sensitive items. We usually ask customers to provide ~200-400 golden prompts for the initial eval if possible.
[02:40] Marta Villanueva: We can do 300. We'll include a mix: short queries, long context summarization, table extraction.
[02:48] Priya Kapoor: Great. For scoring: human raters on golden set with 1-5 scale covering correctness, hallucination, and formatting. Automated metrics include exact match, token-level accuracy for structured fields, ROUGE/BLEU for free-text similarity where appropriate, and a custom hallucination-rate metric computed as flagged outputs / total.
[03:12] Samir Patel: Can you share what weights you suggest for those scores?
[03:18] Jordan Meyer: We typically weight hallucination as highest priority — e.g., 40% hallucination (lower is better), 30% human quality, 20% automated similarity, 10% latency/cost bucket. But weights are negotiable per customer.
[03:36] Priya Kapoor: For Lyra we suggested a pass threshold of aggregate score >= 85/100 with hallucination < 2% and format errors < 1%.
[03:48] Marta Villanueva: Ok that maps to product needs. About regression tests, how do we keep the suite healthy across model updates?
[03:56] Chris Lang: We version the golden set and store ground-truth labels in the eval harness. Each model roll deploy triggers the regression suite — smoke checks first, then full golden set. Any regression > specified delta (e.g., drop >3 points in aggregate score) blocks the rollout or triggers a canary.
[04:18] Elise Cho: How are human raters managed? Are you using in-house or third-party?
[04:24] Jordan Meyer: Typically we recommend a hybrid: initial human labeling with your SMEs for domain accuracy, then trained raters for larger sample. We can help connect to vendors or support your internal team.
[04:38] Ravi Iyer: Security questions: data residency and KMS — we need to keep PII out of Redwood-hosted logs for the pilot. Can you confirm options?
[04:48] Priya Kapoor: Yes — Redwood hosted has optional log scrubbing and data retention controls; for stricter needs we can run Dedicated or Private with customer-managed KMS. We'll share the SOC2/ISO docs.
[05:02] Samir Patel: For the smoke run and pilot, what workload sizing do you recommend?
[05:08] Chris Lang: Smoke: 500–1,000 representative prompts over 48 hours to get latency/cost signal. Pilot: 5,000–15,000 prompts depending on concurrency target. If you want throughput testing, we can simulate 100–500 rps in a separate performance run.
[05:28] Marta Villanueva: If we do performance runs, does that require Dedicated hardware?
[05:33] Chris Lang: Not necessarily; hosted can do burst tests but Dedicated gives more predictable p95/p99. For production-level load tests we often use a dedicated node pool in Redwood Dedicated.
[05:46] Elise Cho: We're also worried about format fidelity for table extraction. If the model outputs CSV vs JSON inconsistently, that's a showstopper. How do you validate format?
[05:56] Jordan Meyer: We run schema validators: parse output against JSON schemas, count parse failures, and include format error rates in the automated metrics. We also include toy transforms to catch subtle deviations in field names.
[06:12] Samir Patel: Are these validators part of the Redwood Optimize toolkit?
[06:16] Chris Lang: Yes, the eval harness we share integrates those checks. It can run on your infra or ours.
[06:24] Marta Villanueva: On hallucination checks, do you also use external tools like fact-checking against internal DB?
[06:30] Jordan Meyer: We can plug in knowledge-grounding checks — call out to your internal vector DB or knowledge base to see if answers match referenced facts. If there is mismatch, it's flagged. That requires access to the KB snapshot for the POC.
[06:44] Ravi Iyer: We won't give production DB access; we can provide an anonymized snapshot.
[06:48] Priya Kapoor: That works for the eval. Regarding timeline, after we get the golden prompts and sample corpus, Redwood will run smoke in 48 hours and send results. Pilot kickoff can be within one week after that depending on findings.
[07:02] Elise Cho: Walk us through a typical regression result report.
[07:07] Chris Lang: Report includes: aggregate scores (human/auto), hallucination rate, format error rate, per-prompt diffs highlighting failures, latency/cost breakdown (token counts, p50/p95/p99), and suggested mitigations (prompt engineering, quantization/model variant, or routing). We'll share a sample report.
[07:28] Samir Patel: On model variants — can you fallback to smaller models automatically if latency spikes?
[07:34] Priya Kapoor: Yes, routing policies allow fallback to compatible lower-latency model variants; Redwood Console shows per-route cost/loss tradeoffs. We'll demo this in the pilot.
[07:46] Marta Villanueva: For the smoke run, what's the expected cost? Ballpark.
[07:51] Jordan Meyer: Smoke is small — under a few hundred dollars typically, depends on token sizes. We'll provide a cost estimate in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[08:03] Elise Cho: How do you handle evaluation randomness? We see variability across seeds.
[08:09] Chris Lang: We control sampling parameters — temperature/beam/stop tokens — and run multiple seeds. The reproducibility section of the report will show confidence intervals. For gating we look at median performance across runs and require no regression beyond delta threshold.
[08:28] Samir Patel: When you say human rating 200 samples, is that enough statistically to detect tiny hallucination regressions?
[08:35] Jordan Meyer: For small deltas you need larger samples. For initial gating 200–400 is typical; if you need higher sensitivity we expand the sample or increase automated test coverage.
[08:47] Marta Villanueva: Can we include adversarial prompts in golden set to stress hallucination?
[08:52] Priya Kapoor: Absolutely — include adversarial and edge cases; that's critical.
[08:58] Elise Cho: On the scoring approach, can you walk through an example calculation?
[09:04] Jordan Meyer: Example: Golden set of 300 prompts. For each prompt we compute: Hallucination flag (0/1), human quality score (1-5 normalized to 0-100), format pass (0/1), automated similarity (0-100). Weighted aggregate = 0.4*(100 - hallucination_rate_percent) + 0.3*(avg_human_score) + 0.2*(avg_auto_sim) + 0.1*(latency_score). Convert to 0-100 scale; threshold >=85 passes.
[09:34] Samir Patel: Latency score how calculated?
[09:37] Chris Lang: Latency score is a bucketed penalty — if p50 <= target then full points, p50 slightly above target loses small fraction, p95/p99 violations have larger penalty. We include cost tradeoff in notes.
[09:52] Marta Villanueva: About format checks for table extraction — can we add strict schema matching as a hard gate?
[09:58] Priya Kapoor: Yes, format schema mismatch can be a hard blocker for rollouts. We can set it in the gating policy.
[10:05] Elise Cho: What about regression noise — do you allow baseline drift over time?
[10:10] Jordan Meyer: We track historical baselines; small drifts trigger alerts and a review. Significant drifts (> specified delta) are treated as regressions. We recommend monthly recalibration of golden set to capture data drift.
[10:24] Samir Patel: Ok. Let's talk about test harness access. Do you give us a repo?
[10:30] Chris Lang: We'll share a GitHub repo with the eval harness and a Docker image for local runs. We'll also provide a hosted endpoint if you prefer not to run locally.
[10:40] Marta Villanueva: Can we run the harness on our CI to enforce gates?
[10:45] Jordan Meyer: Yes, it's CI-friendly; you can plug it into your pipeline to block merges based on eval results.
[10:52] Elise Cho: On hallucination detection, do you also compute hallucination severity? Like minor versus critical.
[10:58] Chris Lang: We tag severity — critical hallucinations are factual contradictions or invented citations that could mislead users; minor ones are wording differences. Severity weights into the hallucination metric.
[11:10] Samir Patel: Is there an example of the 'per-prompt diffs' you mentioned?
[11:15] Jordan Meyer: The report shows original prompt, baseline output, candidate output, diff highlights, and reason flags (format failure, hallucination, omission).
[11:28] Priya Kapoor: We'll share a template report. Also, we recommend a separate regression suite for non-regression checks: tokenization consistency, kv cache behavior (K V cache), and prompt truncation edge cases.
[11:44] Marta Villanueva: You said KV cache — sometimes transcripts show it as K V cache, is that going to cause confusion in logs?
[11:50] Chris Lang: Ha, yeah transcription sometimes splits it — in logs we use consistent naming.
[11:56] Elise Cho: Any gotchas on deploying private vs hosted for the POC?
[12:01] Priya Kapoor: Hosted is fastest. Private/VPC is recommended if you require no data leaving your VPC or specific KMS. Private has longer lead time.
[12:12] Ravi Iyer: If we need Private, what's the lead time?
[12:17] Priya Kapoor: Typically 4-8 weeks for on-prem or VPC plans depending on network reviews; Dedicated is faster (1-2 weeks) if cloud-only.
[12:28] Samir Patel: For the pilot, can we start hosted plus a plan for Dedicated later?
[12:32] Priya Kapoor: That's our common path — start hosted for speed, move to Dedicated if you need predictable capacity or isolation.
[12:40] Marta Villanueva: Regarding golden prompts, if we provide 300 prompts, how many are used for human rating vs automated?
[12:47] Jordan Meyer: We typically reserve ~200 for human labeling and keep ~100 for automated regression. You can adjust.
[12:55] Elise Cho: Are annotations stored in your console for audit?
[13:00] Chris Lang: Yes, annotation metadata and audit trail are stored and can be exported; retention configurable per account.
[13:08] Samir Patel: Does Redwood support multi-model A/B evaluation?
[13:12] Jordan Meyer: Yes — the harness can score multiple model outputs for the same prompt set and produce side-by-side comparisons.
[13:20] Marta Villanueva: For the pilot, we want to see model comparisons: open model A vs quantized variant vs Redwood-verified variant. Is that straightforward?
[13:28] Chris Lang: Absolutely. We'll include variants and quantization profiles in the comparison.
[13:34] Elise Cho: How do you surface hallucination examples for engineering triage?
[13:39] Priya Kapoor: The report has a 'Top hallucination reasons' section with examples and suggested mitigations (prompt guardrails, grounding, using model with stronger factuality).
[13:50] Samir Patel: Any recommended prompt engineering patterns for Lyra's use-case (bio summaries)?
[13:56] Jordan Meyer: Use explicit instructions for citation behavior: ask model to state 'I don't know' when uncertain. Provide grounding context where possible and include format templates.
[14:08] Marta Villanueva: We'll prepare templates. For the human evaluation rubric, can you share a sample?
[14:13] Chris Lang: Yes — we'll send a rubric: criteria include factuality (1-5), completeness (1-5), format adherence (pass/fail), confidence (1-5). We'll also include labeling guidelines.
[14:26] Elise Cho: On scoring, do you normalize human scores? Some raters are harsh.
[14:31] Jordan Meyer: We calibrate raters with anchor examples, compute inter-rater agreement, and normalize scores if needed.
[14:40] Samir Patel: For the pilot workload, do you recommend warm cache runs to reflect steady-state?
[14:45] Chris Lang: Yes, run warm-up traffic to prime KV caches and then measure steady-state latency and cost.
[14:52] Marta Villanueva: Any specific tokenization quirks for biomedical terms?
[14:58] Jordan Meyer: Some long chemical names tokenize oddly; we recommend pre-tokenization checks and maybe subword merging strategies to avoid weird truncations.
[15:08] Elise Cho: About reporting frequency — will you provide daily updates during the smoke/pilot?
[15:13] Priya Kapoor: For the smoke run we'll send an initial signal within 24 hours and a full smoke report after 48 hours. During pilot we can do daily dashboards.
[15:23] Ravi Iyer: Security docs — can you send SOC2 + network diagram?
[15:27] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we'll attach SOC2, ISO, and a sample network diagram in the follow-up email.
[15:36] Samir Patel: How do you handle PII accidental leakage in model outputs?
[15:41] Chris Lang: We apply scrubbers on ingested samples for pilot and can configure output scrubbing. Also, for Private deployments the data never leaves your VPC.
[15:52] Marta Villanueva: On tooling, is there a UI to inspect per-prompt results?
[15:56] Jordan Meyer: Redwood Console has per-route dashboards and a per-prompt explorer to filter failures and annotate.
[16:04] Elise Cho: Let's define acceptance criteria clearly for the POC.
[16:09] Priya Kapoor: Proposed acceptance: 1) Aggregate score >=85, 2) Hallucination < 2% on golden set, 3) Format error rate < 1% for structured outputs, 4) p50 latency <= 350ms for 512-token baseline, and 5) cost per 1k tokens under agreed budget bucket. If any hard gate fails (format), rollout is blocked.
[16:34] Samir Patel: That looks good. We'll review and confirm.
[16:39] Marta Villanueva: About human eval, will Redwood do the labeling if we lack capacity?
[16:43] Priya Kapoor: We can help run initial human labeling or assist with vendor selection. Costs for human labeling are additional.
[16:52] Elise Cho: Can you put those acceptance criteria in writing?
[16:55] Priya Kapoor: Yes — included in next steps.
[17:00] Samir Patel: Let's talk about timeline: if we give prompts by Monday, what is realistic?
[17:05] Chris Lang: If we get the corpus Monday (7/28), smoke can run 48 hours and results by Wednesday (7/30), pilot kickoff the next week (8/4) pending results.
[17:18] Marta Villanueva: That timeline fits our internal roadmap.
[17:22] Ravi Iyer: Security review timeline? We'll start it in parallel.
[17:26] Priya Kapoor: Great. We'll send security pack and request network contacts.
[17:33] Elise Cho: Any more questions from Redwood?
[17:36] Jordan Meyer: One ask: include several adversarial prompts that target hallucination in biomedical claims.
[17:41] Marta Villanueva: Will do.
[17:44] Priya Kapoor: Okay, recap of next steps and action items…
[17:48] [SUMMARY & RECAP by Priya Kapoor]
[17:50] Priya Kapoor: Redwood: share golden prompt template, benchmark spreadsheet, sample report, SOC2 docs; Lyra: provide 300 golden prompts, sample corpus, security contact. Aim to run smoke ASAP once artifacts in.
[18:03] Samir Patel: Thanks all, we'll align internally and get artifacts to you.
[18:08] Elise Cho: Thanks. Looking forward to the report.
[18:12] Priya Kapoor: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with links (repo, spreadsheet, and report template).
[18:20] [END CALL]
